demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Making any plans for the future
I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
The world is a dangerous place
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

issues.item: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: 'Perpetrator' cues are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being an unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one; this wording implies an assaultive interpersonal trauma rather than bereavement-related PTSD.

issues.item: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
issues.explanation: 'Safe seat seeking' fits fear of immediate interpersonal attack or entrapment more than traumatic bereavement. In combination with startle/hypervigilance, it shifts the profile toward assault-type threat rather than loss-related PTSD, with no supporting trauma-specific content elsewhere.

vignette:
Ravi is a 20-year-old writer from a South Asian family, living alone in a small apartment in Chicago. Eight months ago, his older brother, Arun, died suddenly from a cardiac arrest at the age of twenty-four. Ravi had been the one to find him collapsed on the bathroom floor, the paramedics unable to revive him. The memory of that morning is fragmented but searing: the cold tile against his knees, the phone slipping from his hand, the paramedic’s voice saying “I’m sorry” in a tone that sounded rehearsed. What stays with him most is the silence afterward, the apartment feeling hollow in a way he cannot describe.

In the weeks that followed, Ravi stopped making plans. He had been working on a novel, a sprawling family saga, but he closed the document and did not open it again. He told himself he was just taking a break, but the truth was that every attempt to imagine a future felt like a betrayal—or worse, an invitation for more loss. He began asking his roommate, his mother, even his barista whether he seemed okay, needing them to confirm that he was still functioning, still normal. He avoided anything that reminded him of Arun: the corner deli where they used to buy samosas, the playlist they shared, the smell of cardamom. He had come to believe that the world was a fundamentally dangerous place, a place where a healthy twenty-four-year-old could drop dead without warning, and that his own sense of safety had been an illusion. He used to be a happy person, he told his therapist in their first session; now he was always miserable, and he was certain that happiness was something he would never feel again.

Because Ravi saw the world as hostile and unpredictable, he remained on high alert. He could not relax, even in his own apartment, which he had once considered a sanctuary. Ordinary sounds—the hum of the refrigerator, a car door slamming outside—made him jump, his heart racing as if something terrible was about to happen again. He had trouble falling asleep, lying awake for hours listening to the building settle, certain that any creak could be a sign of catastrophe. This constant vigilance, in turn, fed his sense that the world was dangerous; his body’s alarm system told him there was reason to be afraid, so there must be.

His avoidance strategies deepened the cycle. By refusing to make plans, he never gave himself the chance to experience a positive future, which only confirmed his belief that there was nothing to look forward to. By seeking reassurance, he was always reminded of his own fragility, because the words of comfort never lasted. His avoidance of grief reminders meant he never processed the loss, so the world remained a place where loss could strike at any moment. And the more he avoided, the more he jumped at sounds, because his nervous system had no chance to habituate to ordinary life. He started working from home exclusively, telling his editor he needed quiet to write, but the truth was that he could not bear the unpredictability of the outside world. His novel remained unfinished, and his social life shrank to near nothing.

What finally brought Ravi to therapy was a panic attack in a coffee shop when a stranger coughed. He was certain it was a heart attack, certain he was about to die the way Arun had died. He fled, but the attack left him shaken and ashamed. He is most afraid that he will never be able to feel safe again, that the world will always feel like a place where happiness is a prelude to loss. But he is also, quietly, hoping that someone can help him find a way back to the person he used to be—even if he is not sure that person exists anymore.
